1.e4 c6 2.d4.strategy: Builds a two-pawn centre and takes the most space. Black's 2...d5 attacks e4 at once, and White then decides the character of the game: open piece play, a closed centre where White holds the space, or a balanced structure after an exchange. The cost is a centre that Black challenges straight away.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move and keeps the d-pawn flexible, so White can still head for the main line or choose faster development with the knights. The price is that the knight occupies c3, which rules out a set-up with the c-pawn on c3.

1.e4 c6 2.c4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Accelerated Panov Attack
1.e4 c6 2.c4.background: After 2...d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.d4 it transposes to the Panov–Botvinnik Attack, named after Vasily Panov and world champion Mikhail Botvinnik, which otherwise begins 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4. The position after 2.c4 can also arise from the English Opening, after 1.c4 c6 2.e4.
1.e4 c6 2.c4.strategy: Controls d5 in advance, so that White can meet 2...d5 by exchanging and then striking at the centre with d4, aiming for open, active play. The move develops no piece, and Black can sidestep these structures by building the centre differently.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight toward the centre and keeps the d-pawn flexible, aiming at quick development. It leaves e4 undefended for the moment, so White has to deal with the attack on it after 2...d5, but the queen's knight stays free to choose its square.

1.e4 c6 2.d3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Breyer Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d3.background: White more often answers 2...d5 with 3.Nd2, but the queenless line 3.Nf3 dxe4 4.dxe4 Qxd1+ 5.Kxd1 gained attention in the 21st century.
1.e4 c6 2.d3.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn and prepares quiet development of the pieces. It is sound but unambitious: White postpones the fight for d4 and aims for a slow, flexible game in which the queens often stay on the board.

1.e4 c6 2.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 with pawn support. The move is sound but rare: it takes c3 from the queen's knight, which can no longer defend e4 from there.

1.e4 c6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2 and keeps d4 and Nc3 in reserve. It is sound but slow: after 2...d5 the e4-pawn needs an answer at once, and the bishop on g2 bears on the centre only after that pawn has been exchanged or advanced.

1.e4 c6 2.b3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Euwe Attack
1.e4 c6 2.b3.background: Max Euwe won with it against Richard Réti in the third game of their match in Amsterdam in June 1920.
1.e4 c6 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2 on the long diagonal and fights for the centre from a distance instead of occupying it. It leaves Black free to build a broad centre, and White has to undermine that centre later.

1.e4 c6 2.f3.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn but takes f3 from the king's knight and weakens the e1–h4 and a7–g1 diagonals. Black can also answer 2...e5, aiming at the dark squares around White's king.

1.e4 c6 2.e5.strategy: Pushes the e-pawn before d4 can support it, so 2...d6 hits the pawn at once. White has gained space only if Black allows it.

1.e4 c6 2.Ne2.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Bohemian Attack
1.e4 c6 2.Ne2.strategy: Blocks the f1-bishop and does not defend e4, so 2...d5 attacks the pawn at once. The knight covers d4 and can reroute to g3, but White develops more slowly than after the natural knight moves.

1.e4 c6 2.Be2.strategy: A slow developing move that neither supports e4 nor prepares d4, and takes e2 from the queen and the g1-knight. Black takes the centre with 2...d5, and the bishop on e2 does nothing against it.

1.e4 c6 2.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 but blocks the d2-pawn, so d4 is impossible until the bishop moves again. Black takes the centre with 2...d5, and after ...dxe4 Bxe4 the bishop is hit by ...Nf6 with gain of time.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Hillbilly Attack
1.e4 c6 2.Bc4.background: Simon Williams attributes the name to National Master Jack Young, who allegedly used it for the move's unrefined nature and claimed to have invented it in 1988. It emerged as a surprise weapon in online blitz because of the gambit 3.Bb3 after 2...d5, advocated by Williams.
1.e4 c6 2.Bc4.strategy: Aims at f7 but the bishop is hit by 2...d5, and after 3.exd5 cxd5 it has to move again, losing time. White gets no lasting initiative for the tempo and Black takes the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.g4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Spike Variation
1.e4 c6 2.g4.strategy: Advances on the kingside without developing a piece and weakens the squares around the king. Black strikes at e4 with 2...d5, and the g4-pawn becomes a target for the c8-bishop and for ...h5.

1.e4 c6 2.b4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Labahn Attack
1.e4 c6 2.b4.strategy: Gains queenside space without developing and leaves the b4-pawn unsupported. Black takes the centre at once and can harass the unprotected pawn.

1.e4 c6 2.f4.strategy: Gains kingside space and prepares Nf3 and e5, but weakens the e1–h4 diagonal and the e3-square. It does nothing for e4, so 2...d5 attacks an undefended pawn and Black develops easily.

1.e4 c6 2.Qf3.strategy: Defends e4 but takes f3 from the king's knight and exposes the queen early. After 2...d5 the c8-bishop can hit the queen from g4, so Black develops with gain of time.

1.e4 c6 2.Qe2.strategy: Defends e4 but shuts in the f1-bishop and takes e2 from the king's knight, while d4 remains unprepared. Black takes the centre with 2...d5 and develops freely.

1.e4 c6 2.Qg4.strategy: Loses time: after 2...d5 the c8-bishop attacks the queen, which must retreat, and 3.exd5? even loses it to 3...Bxg4. Black gets the centre and development with tempo.

1.e4 c6 2.Qh5.strategy: Eyes f7, but the queen is exposed: 2...Nf6 attacks it and the e4-pawn at the same time, and Black develops with gain of time.

1.e4 c6 2.Nh3.strategy: Develops the king's knight to the rim, where it neither defends e4 nor supports d4. After 2...d5 the c8-bishop also hits the knight, and ...Bxh3 gxh3 would double White's h-pawns.

1.e4 c6 2.Na3.strategy: A rim knight that helps neither e4 nor d4. It heads for c4, but 2...d5 takes that square away at once, and White has lost time without a plan.

1.e4 c6 2.a3.strategy: A slow rook-pawn move that neither develops a piece nor fights for the centre. Black takes space at once with 2...d5 and has gained a tempo.

1.e4 c6 2.a4.strategy: Gains queenside space slowly and weakens b4, but does nothing against 2...d5, which takes the centre with a tempo against e4.

1.e4 c6 2.h3.strategy: A waiting move that only prevents ...Bg4 later. It costs a tempo and does nothing about 2...d5, so Black takes the centre while White has not developed.

1.e4 c6 2.h4.strategy: Gains a little kingside space but neither develops a piece nor helps the centre. Black takes the centre with 2...d5, attacking the undefended e4-pawn, and White is a tempo behind.

1.e4 c6 2.Ke2.strategy: Gives up castling for good and leaves the king in the centre, with no gain in space or development. Black plays 2...d5 and opens the centre against the exposed king.

1.e4 c6 2.Bb5.strategy: Hangs the bishop: the c6-pawn simply takes it with 2...cxb5.

1.e4 c6 2.Ba6.strategy: Hangs the bishop for nothing: 2...bxa6 or 2...Nxa6 wins it at once.

1.e4 c6.name: Caro–Kann Defence
1.e4 c6.background: Named after the English player Horatio Caro and the Austrian Marcus Kann, who analysed it in 1886. Kann had beaten Jacques Mieses with it in 24 moves at the German Chess Congress in Hamburg in May 1885.

1.e4 c6 2.b4 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once, the way the Caro-Kann is meant to be played. White's early b-pawn advance does nothing for the fight over the centre, so Black simply gets the usual solid structure.

1.e4 c6 2.b4 e5.strategy: Takes the centre with the e-pawn instead and opens the bishop's diagonal towards the b4 pawn, which nothing defends. It is a sharper choice than ...d5, because the e5 pawn itself soon becomes a target and Black must look after both pawns.

1.e4 c6 2.b4 a5.strategy: Attacks the advanced b-pawn at once and makes White decide how to keep the queenside together. White must be careful: defending with a3 and recapturing on b4 with the a-pawn drops the rook on a1 to a capture on the open file.

1.e4 c6 2.b4 d5 3.b5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Labahn Attack, Double Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.b4 d5 3.b5.strategy: A double gambit: Black can take the b5 pawn with ...cxb5 or the e4 pawn with ...dxe4. White has nothing developed and gets no real compensation for a pawn, which makes this a try for surprise rather than a sound plan.

1.e4 c6 2.b4 d5 3.exd5.strategy: The sensible way to play on: trading pawns lets White develop freely, with the bishop aimed along the long diagonal. Black recaptures with the c-pawn and keeps a pawn in the centre, so White gains nothing, but the early b-pawn move is no liability and the game is level.

1.e4 c6 2.b4 d5 3.e5.strategy: Gains space, but with no pawn on d4 behind it the e5 pawn is poorly supported, and ...c5 at once hits the b4 pawn as well. White has done nothing for the centre with the b-pawn and is the one who has to prove the advance sound.

1.e4 c6 2.b4 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and defends e4, but if Black takes the pawn, the recapturing knight stands on e4 with no protection and can be attacked with tempo. White ends up reacting to Black's development rather than leading.

1.e4 c6 2.b4 e5 3.Bb2.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Labahn Attack, Polish Variation
1.e4 c6 2.b4 e5 3.Bb2.strategy: The point of 2.b4: the bishop comes out on the long diagonal and attacks the e5 pawn, which nothing defends. White pays with the loose b4 pawn, so this is a gambit for quick development and the initiative.

1.e4 c6 2.b4 e5 3.a3.strategy: Guards the b4 pawn so that the bishop cannot take it, but costs a tempo and develops nothing. The e5 pawn is left alone and Black can claim the centre at once, so White has some queenside space and little else to show for it.

1.e4 c6 2.b4 e5 3.Nf3.strategy: Attacks e5 with a developing move and leaves the b4 pawn loose: if Black takes it with the bishop, White wins e5 back and the pawns are level. Black has other ways to defend e5, and the bishop's long-diagonal pressure that makes the gambit work is missing.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4 d5.strategy: Strikes at once: the d5 pawn is protected twice, by the c-pawn and the queen, so the bishop has to leave the diagonal. Black gains central space with a tempo and loses nothing by it.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4 e5.strategy: Takes the centre with the king's pawn instead of striking at the bishop. Black has to keep f7 in mind, since the bishop and a queen on h5 both aim at it, and White develops with a tempo by attacking the e5 pawn. Sound, but less forcing than the central strike.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4 e6.strategy: A solid set-up that prepares a central pawn chain and keeps White's bishop under threat of being driven back. The cost is the bishop on c8, which is shut in behind the e6 pawn, and White can build a full centre before Black has a say.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4 d5 3.Bb3.strategy: Keeps the bishop on the diagonal towards f7 and leaves the e4 pawn en prise as a gambit, instead of losing a tempo after an exchange on d5. White offers a pawn for quick play against the Black king.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4 d5 3.exd5.strategy: Trades the e-pawn for the d-pawn and gives up the centre. Black retakes with a pawn that hits the bishop, so White loses a tempo and has no centre pawn to show for it, and Black develops comfortably.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4 d5 3.Bd3.strategy: Drops the bishop back to d3, where it blocks its own d-pawn. Black takes on e4, the bishop has to recapture there, and a knight move then hits it again, so White loses time twice for no compensation.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4 d5 3.Bb3 dxe4.strategy: Accepts the gambit: Black wins a clean pawn and removes White's central pawn. The cost is that the bishop now eyes f7, so Black must develop with that square in mind.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4 d5 3.Bb3 e6.strategy: Declines the pawn and backs up d5, so the bishop on b3 and the e4 pawn find nothing to win. Black gets a solid centre; the cost is the light-squared bishop, which is shut in behind its own pawns.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4 d5 3.Bb3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and keeps the tension instead of capturing, the knight adding a second attacker to e4. Black gives up the extra pawn that taking would keep, and White can drive the knight back with the e-pawn and gain space.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4 d5 3.Bb3 dxe4 4.Qh5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Hillbilly Attack, Schaeffer Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.Bc4 d5 3.Bb3 dxe4 4.Qh5.strategy: Brings the queen to join the bishop against f7, which only the king defends. There is no mate threat, but Black does well to blunt the attack first and only then complete development. White's compensation is time and activity for the pawn.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4 d5 3.Bb3 dxe4 4.Nc3.strategy: Attacks the e4 pawn with a developing move while the bishop keeps f7 under pressure. White plays for quick development rather than an immediate attack, and Black has to decide whether to hold the pawn or to return it for a comfortable game.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4 d5 3.Bb3 dxe4 4.Qe2.strategy: Attacks the e4 pawn with the queen and keeps the other pieces flexible. Black can defend the pawn with a developing move and keep the extra pawn, so White has an attack on a pawn but no lead in development.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Accelerated Panov Attack
1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5.strategy: Strikes at the e4-pawn at once, the thematic Caro–Kann break, before White can support the centre. White then chooses how the pawns are exchanged, and in the main lines ends up with an isolated d-pawn, accepted for fast development and attacking chances.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d6.strategy: Postpones the ...d5 break for a compact set-up with pawns on c6 and d6. It is solid but passive: with pawns on c4, d4 and e4 White gets a clear space advantage, and Black has to catch up from behind.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a French-style pawn chain. It is sound, but it shuts in the c8-bishop that the Caro–Kann set-up usually keeps free, and White's extra space on c4 gives the more comfortable play.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 e5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Accelerated Panov Attack, Open Variation
1.e4 c6 2.c4 e5.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn instead of striking at e4 with ...d5. The c6-pawn takes the natural square from the knight, so Black must keep e5 defended, and with c4 and e4 covering d5 the freeing ...d5 is hard to achieve. The position stays solid but passive.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, with ...c6 already played. It is sound but leaves the centre to White: with pawns on c4, d4 and e4 White has a clear space advantage, and Black must find the right moment for ...d5.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, far from the centre, aiming at c7 or b4. It does nothing against a broad pawn centre, so White simply builds one while c4 and e4 keep their grip on d5.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 Qc7.strategy: Eyes e5 along the b8–h2 diagonal but brings the queen out before any piece is developed. White takes the centre at leisure, and Bf4 can later gain time against the queen.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 Qb6.strategy: Aims at b2 and d4, but b2 is guarded by the c1-bishop, so nothing is threatened. The queen leaves the back rank before any piece is developed, and White builds a full centre in comfort.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 Qa5.strategy: Eyes the a5–e1 diagonal and prepares ...e5, but develops nothing. White gains time developing, and the queen stays exposed to harassment by ideas such as Bd2.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 Nh6.strategy: A rim knight aiming at f5 that leaves d5 uncontested. Once White plays d4, Bxh6 gxh6 threatens to wreck the kingside pawns, so Black must spend more time on the knight or the kingside.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 but runs into 3.e5, which drives the knight away. White gains space and tempi, and Black's pieces stand awkwardly in the face of a broad centre.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 against the c4-pawn but spends a tempo on an edge pawn. White builds a broad centre while ...d5 is still unplayed.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 a5.strategy: A wing move that gains no useful space and touches neither the centre nor the d5 square. White builds on the pawns already on c4 and e4.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, but the c6-pawn blocks that bishop's diagonal toward e4, and ...d5 still has to be played. White meanwhile takes the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 f6.strategy: Blocks the knight's natural square and weakens e6 and the king's diagonal. It does nothing against the pawns on c4 and e4, and White takes the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 g5.strategy: Loosens the kingside for good and makes the pawn a target: after d4 the c1-bishop attacks g5, and holding it with ...h6 costs another tempo against White's full centre.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 h6.strategy: A prophylactic pawn move that takes g5 from the bishop but develops nothing and leaves d5 uncontested. White builds a broad centre.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 h5.strategy: Gains space on the wing but weakens g5 and the kingside, and develops nothing. White keeps the centre and develops freely.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 c5.strategy: The second step of the c-pawn gives a Sicilian-like structure but costs a tempo, and with c4 and e4 White already controls d5. A quiet bind follows easily.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn without real compensation. After 3.cxb5 cxb5 4.Bxb5 White is a clean pawn up, and the open c-file and ...Bb7 against e4 do not make up for it.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 f5.strategy: Offers the f-pawn for nothing: 3.exf5 simply wins it, and the king and the e6-square are left weakened with no development in return.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.exd5.strategy: The most direct way to settle the tension. White takes first and lets Black choose the recapture: a pawn recapture leaves c4 pressing on d5, and a queen recapture runs into that pawn.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5.strategy: Trades the c-pawn instead and keeps the e-pawn, which Black's recapture then attacks. White gives up the pressure on d5 from c4 in return for an open c-file and lively piece play.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.e5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Toikkanen Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.e5.strategy: A gambit that pushes the e-pawn past d5 to gain space, but it gives up the e-pawn's hold on d5 that 2.c4 was played for. The pawn on e5 has no pawn or piece behind it and becomes a target, while Black's centre stays intact.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 cxd5.strategy: The natural recapture, and it hits e4 at once. White has to decide how to meet the attack on the pawn, and Black has a sound central pawn and an open c-file for the rooks.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 Qxd5.strategy: Hangs the queen: the pawn on e4 attacks d5 and takes the queen for a pawn. The recapture looks natural but Black has no compensation for the loss.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 Nf6.strategy: Skips the recapture to attack d5 and e4 with the knight, offering a pawn for development. White can take on c6 and be a pawn up, and Black's lead in development has to pay for it.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Qb3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Accelerated Panov Attack, Van Weersel Attack
1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Qb3.strategy: Adds a second attacker to d5 and eyes b7, but brings the queen out early. Black can defend d5 with ordinary development and the queen then has to find a new post, so White gains little from the double attack.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.exd5.strategy: Takes the pawn and removes the attacker of e4 at the same time. White is a pawn up for the moment, but the pawn on d5 is hard to hold. The trade leaves White with an isolated d-pawn, to be paid for with piece activity.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops and defends e4 at once, adding a second attacker to d5 for a later capture. White keeps the choice of how to open the centre, but takes no pawn, so Black can equalise easily.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5.strategy: The natural recapture: the queen stays at home and Black keeps a pawn on d5. That pawn is attacked by c4 and defended once, so Black must be ready to meet the exchange on d5 by winning the pawn back with a piece.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Accelerated Panov Attack, Pseudo-Scandinavian
1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Hangs the queen: the pawn on c4 attacks d5 and takes the queen for a pawn. Black has no compensation for the loss.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.exd5 Nf6.strategy: Develops instead of recapturing: the knight attacks d5 a second time and Black can still retake with the c-pawn later. White can take on c6 and be a pawn up, but then Black has central control and quick development to pay for it.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.cxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn on d5 and is a pawn up, though only for the moment. The pawn on d5 is hard to hold, and the trade has cleared White's c- and e-pawns away from the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.d4.strategy: Meets the d5 pawn with a central strike instead of capturing it. White gets a broad centre of c- and d-pawns against Black's lone d-pawn, and plays for pressure on it and active pieces, while Black plays for quick development and freeing exchanges.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops and keeps the d5 pawn under double attack without resolving the tension. Black can release it by taking on c4, when the bishop retakes at once, or defend it with a developing move; White keeps a normal game but has committed to no structure.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.cxd5 Nf6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Accelerated Panov Attack, Modern Variation
1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.cxd5 Nf6.strategy: Attacks the extra pawn, which White usually cannot hold. Black regains it with a developing move, and White is left with an isolated d-pawn that is a weakness in the endgame and has to be paid for with piece activity.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.cxd5 Qxd5.strategy: Retakes at once with the queen, winning the pawn back and simplifying the structure. The queen comes out early and is hit by a developing knight move, so White gains time and keeps the initiative.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.cxd5 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece before regaining the pawn, but the knight does not itself attack d5. White gets time to defend the pawn with a developing move, so Black's recovery is slower and less forceful than with a direct attack on it.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once and challenges e4, which White's modest move has to meet. Black gets a firm claim to the centre while White prepares a quiet set-up.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 e5.strategy: Claims the centre with the king's pawn first and keeps the choice of how to support it. The game stays quiet and manoeuvring: White builds a compact set-up with a fianchettoed bishop, Black holds a broad, solid centre.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 e6.strategy: Builds a solid pawn centre and stays flexible. The cost is the bishop on c8, which is shut in behind the e6 pawn, the very problem the c6 pawn was meant to avoid, so Black's development is a little slower.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2.strategy: Defends e4 a second time, so the pawn can be exchanged and retaken with the d-pawn, and avoids the early queen trade down the d-file. White keeps the queens on and a flexible set-up with a solid pawn chain.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Accepts that Black may take on e4: after the exchange the queens face each other on the d-file and can come off, leaving a level endgame with White's king stuck in the centre. A respectable way to play for a long manoeuvring game without risk.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move, so White can retake on e4 with the knight and avoid the queen trade. The knight can be driven away by ...d4, which gives Black more space in the centre, but White's position stays playable.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 g6.strategy: Chooses a fianchetto set-up that presses on the centre from a distance instead of occupying it with the e-pawn. Black keeps the pawn structure flexible and plays for a long manoeuvring game.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 e5.strategy: Takes the centre with a second pawn and keeps the tension on e4. Black builds a broad pawn centre and a solid set-up where White's slow plan is a reversed version of Black's own, leaving a long game in which the central pawns decide.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 dxe4.strategy: Settles the tension in the centre and lets White choose how to retake. After the exchange the d-file is open and the pawn structure is simple; the knight on d2 has taken a less active square than on f3, and Black can follow up with ...e5.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 g6 4.Ngf3.strategy: Brings the second knight out to its natural square, where it covers e5 and d4 and starts clearing the way for castling. With the d3 and e4 pawns behind it, White builds a solid centre and keeps a flexible plan.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 g6 4.g3.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto first and decides on the second knight later. The bishop on g2 will support the centre from behind, and the move keeps White's options open for the kingside knight and for a later central break.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 g6 4.d4.strategy: Takes the full centre at once and gives up the slow set-up. White gets space, but with d3 played and the knight on d2 it has lost time compared with an ordinary opening, so Black exchanges on e4 and equalises without trouble.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 g6 4.Ngf3 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop presses on the long diagonal towards the centre and takes a step towards castling. Black develops without any hurry, since nothing in White's set-up threatens the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 g6 4.Ngf3 Nf6.strategy: Puts a second attacker on the e4 pawn and keeps the choice of the bishop's square open. Black develops with pressure, and White has to decide how to deal with the tension in the centre while the king's bishop is still to come out.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 g6 4.Ngf3 dxe4.strategy: Releases the tension and opens the d-file. White can retake with either the pawn or the knight and gets a comfortable position, since Black has given up the central pawn that was holding the e4 pawn in check.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 g6 4.Ngf3 Bg7 5.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop to g2, where it backs up the centre from behind. White plays by set-up rather than by direct threats, aiming for a slow game in which the pieces rather than the pawns decide.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 g6 4.Ngf3 Bg7 5.Be.strategy: Develops the bishop to its natural square and prepares to castle at once, without committing the g-pawn. It is a harmless set-up, but the bishop does less on e2 than it would on the long diagonal.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 g6 4.Ngf3 Bg7 5.d4.strategy: Builds the broad centre immediately. White gets space and solid pawns on d4 and e4, but the central tension gives Black an easy exchange on e4 and a comfortable game, so the slow set-up has been abandoned for little.

1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 g6 4.Ngf3 Bg7 5.g3.strategy: Stakes a claim to the centre now that the bishop supports it: the e5 pawn is attacked by the knight and defended by the bishop. Black gets a broad pawn centre, and White must decide when to resolve the tension on e4.
Develops the knight with pressure on e4 and prepares to castle. Black keeps the e-pawn back for now and plays for a flexible set-up, leaving White to decide how the central tension is resolved.
Opens the d-file by trading a pawn, with an easy recapture for White. Black gets a simple position, but the central pawn is gone, so the bishop on g2 will work on a more open diagonal.
Completes the fianchetto and gets the king ready to castle. The bishop stands behind the f3 knight and will work along the long diagonal once the centre opens, so White waits for Black to commit.
Gives the d4 square extra protection and prepares a later d4. It is a sound but slow waiting move, and White still has to complete development, so it adds little to the fight for the centre.

Adds a second defender to e4 and keeps the queen on a flexible square. It is sound but passive: White does nothing to challenge Black's pawn centre and still has the bishop and king to bring into the game.
A flexible development: the knight backs up d5 and c6 and leaves the f-pawn free to advance. It does not take the f6 square, so Black keeps a free hand for the pawn break against White's centre.

The natural development: the knight attacks e4 and clears the way for castling, while the e5 and d5 pawns hold the centre. Black plans a solid game in which a later central break decides, since the position is rich in tension.

Gives up the tension and opens the d-file, so the queens may come off. White retakes comfortably and the bishop on g2 soon eyes the e4 pawn, while Black has released its pressure on e4 and has nothing more than equality to play for.

1.e4 c6 2.g4 d5.strategy: The natural reply: the g-pawn advance does nothing for the centre, so Black strikes at e4 at once. The pawn on g4 is a weakness, and the bishop on c8 already looks at it; White's early flank advance leaves the kingside loose.

1.e4 c6 2.g4 Nf6.strategy: Hits the undefended e4 pawn at once and eyes g4, so White has to commit. Pushing e5 gains space with a tempo on the knight, which then needs a new square; Black is solid but has helped White gain space.

1.e4 c6 2.g4 e5.strategy: Takes the centre with the e-pawn at once, which abandons the idea behind ...c6: a pawn on d5 backed by the c-pawn. The game is sound, but Black does not use the first chance to attack e4, and White gets time to catch up in development.

1.e4 c6 2.g4 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: Guards the e4 pawn and develops, but does nothing about what g4 has created: that pawn is guarded only by the queen, and White's kingside is loose. Black exchanges in the centre and has the easier game.

1.e4 c6 2.g4 d5 3.exd5.strategy: Trades the e-pawn for the d5 pawn at once, so Black cannot win a pawn on e4. After the c-pawn recaptures, the f1 bishop gets a check on b5, and the queen still guards g4 against the c8 bishop. White plays for quick development and has to keep an eye on the loosened kingside.

1.e4 c6 2.g4 d5 3.e5.strategy: Gains space and shuts the c8 bishop out: ...Bf5 runs into the g4 pawn, and ...Bg4 is met by the queen. The price is an advanced, exposed centre and a loose kingside, and Black will attack the advanced pawns at once.

1.e4 c6 2.g4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn and opens the d-file, where the queen now looks at White's d2 pawn, while the bishop on c8 keeps its eye on g4, which only the queen guards. White has to recover the pawn or find compensation at once.

1.e4 c6 2.g4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: The knight eyes e4 and g4, and the c8 bishop looks at g4 as well, so the pawn is attacked twice and guarded only by the queen. White has to support it at once, because pushing e5 just loses it to ...Nxg4. Black develops with tempo and keeps the option of taking on e4.

1.e4 c6 2.g4 d5 3.Nc3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 with a pawn and frees the f8 bishop, but locks the c8 bishop behind the e6 pawn, the piece the Caro-Kann is meant to keep free, and gives up the pressure on g4. Safe and solid, yet it lets White consolidate instead of punishing the flank advance.

1.e4 c6 2.g4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Spike Variation, Scorpion-Grob Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.g4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d3.strategy: Offers a second pawn to open lines for the c1 bishop and hit e4, but after Black takes on d3 and White recaptures, White is a pawn down with a lead in development as the only compensation. The g4 pawn is still a target: a gambit that gives more than it gets.

1.e4 c6 2.g4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4.strategy: Wins the pawn back with the developed knight: material is level and the knight is centralised. The cost is a position the flank advance has already loosened, with the d-file open for Black's queen and g4 guarded only by the queen, so Black has the easier game.

1.e4 c6 2.g4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Qe2.strategy: Attacks e4 a second time and guards the loose g4 pawn from one square. But it blocks the f1 bishop and puts the queen on the e-file in front of the king, and Black can defend e4 with a developing move, so White gains little time.
